preamble: Velar palatalization of [k] to the postalveolar affricate [tʃ] is a widespread historical phonetic shift, typically triggered by following front vowels or the palatal glide [j]. This process, often involving an intermediate palatal stop stage [c], is a defining feature of the Slavic First Palatalization and the development of several Romance languages from Latin. In English, this is seen in the 'ch' of words like 'chin' (from Proto-Germanic *kinnus). In Dravidian, Proto-Dravidian *k became c before front vowels in Tamil, Malayalam and Telugu (*kewi 'ear' > Tamil and Telugu cevi), while Kannada and Tulu keep k (kivi, kebi).

examples.note: Georgian undergoes velar palatalization before high vowels, historically and phonologically: /k/ > [tʃ] before [i], as seen in plural forms and diminutives.
Development before front vowels. E.g., Russian 'četyre' (four) from PIE *kwetwor-.
Old English palatalization before front vowels.

Turkish velar stops /k, ɡ/ are palatalized to [c, ɟ] when adjacent to front vowels /e, i/ in native words. E.g., kedi (cat) [ke.di], kız (girl) [kɯz] vs. gemi (ship) [ɡe.mi]. Also observable in diminutives and derivative affixes.

A defining sound change of the Cholan-Tseltalan branch: Proto-Mayan *k and *k' shifted to /ch/ and /ch'/ in specific phonological contexts. E.g., attested in Tzeltal and Chol. Recent research suggests this change spread through areal contact during the Classic period rather than solely through genetic inheritance.
The ejective counterpart *k' also underwent affrication to ch' in Cholan and Tseltalan languages, confirming the systematic nature of the shift.

examples.from: ကျောင်း kyoṅḥ 'school, monastery'
examples.note: Velar + medial y (and r) palatalized to [tɕ]
Mandinka kèɲè and Xasonka kéɲè keep k. Palatalized reflexes also occur in Maninka-Mori cìɲɛ́ (alongside kìɲɛ́, tìɲɛ́), Koro cɛ̌ⁿ and Koya cɛ̰̀. In Mande orthography c = [tʃ].
Bimson (1976) reconstructs *k for 'man' and 'sand'. The k in 'egg' (Bambara kili) is not palatalized before i.

Telugu palatalizes here, unlike Tamil கெடு keṭu.
